:::{#thm-cdf-derivative-density}
#### A piecewise-smooth CDF has its derivative as a density

If the CDF $\cdf$ of a random variable $X$ is continuous everywhere,
and has a continuous derivative at all but finitely many points,
then $X$ is continuous,
and $\cdf'$ (given any values at the finitely many exceptional points)
is a density of $X$.

:::

::: proof

For events $A \subseteq B$,
$B$ is the disjoint union of $A$ and $B \setminus A$,
so additivity gives $\Pr(A) \le \Pr(B)$.
For any $x$ and $\change > 0$,
$\{X = x\} \subseteq \{x - \change < X \le x\}$, so:

$$
\ba
0
&\le \Pr(X = x)
&& \text{(probabilities are non-negative)} \\
&\le \Pr(x - \change < X \le x)
&& \text{(} \{X = x\} \subseteq \{x - \change < X \le x\} \text{)} \\
&= \cdff{x} - \cdff{x - \change}
&& \text{(additivity, and the definition of the CDF)}
\ea
$$

and $\cdff{x} - \cdff{x - \change} \to 0$ as $\change \downarrow 0$, because $\cdf$ is continuous.
So $\Pr(X = x) = 0$ for every $x$, and $X$ is continuous.
Then, for $a \le b$:

$$
\ba
\Pr(a \le X \le b)
&= \Pr(a < X \le b)
&& \text{(} \Pr(X = a) = 0 \text{)} \\
&= \cdff{b} - \cdff{a}
&& \text{(additivity, and the definition of the CDF)} \\
&= \int_a^b \cdf'(x)\,dx
&& \text{(fundamental theorem of calculus)}
\ea
$$

The last step applies the fundamental theorem of calculus
on each piece of $[a, b]$ between exceptional points,
where $\cdf'$ is continuous,
and joins the pieces using the continuity of $\cdf$ at the exceptional points.
Finally, $\cdf' \ge 0$ wherever it exists, because $\cdf$ is non-decreasing (@thm-cdf-properties).

:::
